title: Slaves or Sons? LLMs, Wisdom, and Writing Instruction
author: Ryan Sinni
summary: Ryan Sinni, an English professor at LeTourneau University, argues that AI cannot exercise prudence and that this matters for the writing classroom. Drawing on Josef Pieper's account of prudence and Shannon Vallor's The AI Mirror, he explains that practical wisdom discerns the good in particular situations and cannot be reduced to casuistry or rule application. The AskDelphi example, which approved eating babies when 'really, really hungry', shows how rule-based systems misapply principles. He then contends that a composition course is a 'reason-giving space' where students learn to stand by their words, and that offloading judgment to an LLM erodes this formation. His own practice is two required one-on-one meetings per essay, trading general instruction for specific feedback. The essay concludes that classroom choices about LLMs flow from contrasting visions of the moral life.
points: Prudence looks both upward toward the good and downward toward the particular situation, so no pre-written rule set can substitute for it.
The AskDelphi failure illustrates how an AI can apply a sound principle to the wrong situation, which is why AI only approximates practical wisdom.
A composition classroom is a 'reason-giving space' in which students learn to justify and stand by their words, and AI cannot stand with them there.
Sinni's concrete response is two required one-on-one conferences per essay, cancelling class in due-date weeks to make room for specific feedback.
Policy on LLMs in writing instruction is downstream of how one defines prudence and the moral life, not merely of detection or rules.
quotes: Prudence is the virtue that discerns and enacts the good in particular situations. As such, it looks in two directions: upward toward the good and downward toward the situation.

In other words, because each situation is unique, no pre-fabricated set of rules can fully account for it. In fact, the attempt to do so was what made AskDelphi say it’s okay to eat babies when you’re really, really hungry.
It should be clear by now that AI programs, despite being touted as practical, cannot exercise practical wisdom. They do not understand their actions.

This is the kind of space the composition classroom can be, especially in a course on argumentative writing. In Wendell Berry’s terms, it can be a place where students are called to stand by their words.
This is why it is so important that our students’ writing advisors be humans and not chatbots: because only humans can be fellow reasoners.
I did this because I believe that the best writing instruction happens in a face-to-face encounter over a particular piece of writing.

In the end, practices in the writing classroom—especially surrounding LLMs—are often downstream from definitions of prudence. To put it more broadly, certain contrasting choices regarding LLMs stem from contrasting visions of the moral life.

But if we believe that rules are no substitute for wisdom, that information is no substitute for formation, and that mindless duty is no substitute for knowing love, we will not choose the prudence of an algorithm over that of a human being fully alive.
